We analyze the $pp \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi \to \phi

This study introduces FPIO, a novel few-shot parsing model designed to generate dependency trees for unseen languages using only a small set of annotated examples. Unlike prior methods that rely on a fixed, pre-defined tree structure, FPIO employs a neural network to learn the tree topology dynamically. We evaluate FPIO across 11 languages, testing scenarios with 10, 50, and 100 training trees. Results indicate that FPIO significantly outperforms previous few-shot approaches, particularly when trained on just 10 trees. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robustness by maintaining consistent performance across languages with varying syntactic complexities.

This study investigates the robustness of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to domain shifts, specifically focusing on speaker and topic variations. We evaluate the impact of training data diversity on model performance by comparing two training strategies: one utilizing a single speaker and topic, and another incorporating multiple speakers and topics. The experiments were conducted using the LibriSpeech dataset, which was modified to include diverse speakers and topics. Results indicate that models trained on varied speakers and topics achieve superior performance compared to those trained on a single domain. Furthermore, we assessed the robustness of these models against unseen speakers and topics by testing them on the VoxCeleb dataset. The findings demonstrate that models trained on diverse data generalize better to unseen speakers and topics than those trained on a single domain.

This study examines the binary frequency of Be stars within the open cluster NGC 2264, utilizing a sample of 100 B-type stars identified via Gaia DR2 data. By applying the same selection criteria used for the Be stars, we identified 100 B-type counterparts. Our analysis reveals that the binary fraction for Be stars in NGC 2264 is 30%, a figure comparable to the 31% binary fraction observed in normal B-type stars. Furthermore, the distributions of orbital periods and projected separations are similar between the two groups. However, Be stars exhibit significantly lower orbital frequencies compared to normal B-type stars. Additionally, the binary fraction for Be stars shows a strong dependence on projected separation, whereas this relationship is not observed for normal B-type stars.

In-domain training is the standard approach for developing Information Extraction (IE) models, yet it demands substantial amounts of labeled data. This study introduces a novel data augmentation technique designed to enhance the performance of Information Extraction Transformer (ITN) models. By employing a multi-task learning framework, the method trains ITN models to simultaneously handle the original task alongside auxiliary tasks, such as token classification and span classification. This approach enables the ITN model to acquire a more comprehensive understanding of the input data. Experimental results indicate that this augmentation strategy improves F1 scores by 1.5% to 2.5% across various datasets. Furthermore, the technique demonstrates robustness by maintaining consistent performance gains even when applied to models trained on small datasets.

This study establishes a Faber-Krahn-type inequality for the Hermite operator, demonstrating that the first eigenvalue is minimized by a half-space. Furthermore, we examine the associated quantitative stability of this inequality.

Neural tangent kernels (NTKs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing the training dynamics of deep learning models. However, their current definition relies on a high-dimensional feature space, which hinders both their interpretability and practical application. This paper introduces a novel approach to NTKs that leverages the inherent structure of the network's weights, resulting in a formulation that is both more interpretable and computationally efficient. We demonstrate that this new NTK framework can be applied to various architectures, including convolutional networks, graph neural networks, and transformers. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees for the convergence of gradient descent when optimizing this NTK-based model.

This study examines the skin effect within a correlated non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson chain, a system where correlations are introduced through a two-site interaction term. We demonstrate that these correlations can be eliminated by applying a local unitary transformation, thereby allowing the system to be analyzed using established non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson methods. Consequently, we find that the correlations do not alter the system's topological properties.

This study investigates the impact of vocal feature convex combinations on the perception of competence and warmth in female speech synthesis. We generated a dataset comprising 1,000 utterances, each created by blending vocal features from three distinct speakers. These utterances were evaluated by 100 participants who rated them on competence and warmth. The results indicate that convex combinations of vocal features yield a perception of competence and warmth that lies between the ratings of the individual speakers.

This study introduces a novel dark matter model based on a $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, where stability is ensured by a discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. The model's framework is extended to incorporate a scalar field that breaks the $U(1)_X$ symmetry, thereby generating a dark photon. This dark photon mediates interactions between dark matter and the Standard Model, with the scalar field itself serving as a dark matter candidate. The research investigates the model's phenomenology, specifically analyzing the constraints imposed by direct detection experiments, collider searches, and the cosmic microwave background.

This study examines the energy levels of triaxial nuclei within the framework of the Bohr-Mottelson collective model, incorporating the effects of minimal length. We demonstrate that the energy spectrum for triaxial nuclei exhibits a linear dependence on angular momentum, a characteristic shared with spherical and axially symmetric systems. Furthermore, we observe that the minimal length parameter significantly influences the energy spectrum, a finding that aligns with experimental data.

This paper examines the construction of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs (GCAPs) with a one-dimensional structure. We establish that a GCAP pair with dimension $N$ is feasible only if $N$ is a perfect square. Furthermore, we present a novel construction method for GCAP pairs of dimension $N^2$ by utilizing two existing GCAP pairs of dimension $N$.

Unsupervised change detection (UCD) is a critical task in remote sensing that identifies alterations between two images without requiring labeled data. This study introduces a novel UCD framework based on a multi-scale feature fusion network, which integrates multi-scale features from a dual-stream architecture to enhance detection accuracy. Furthermore, the paper evaluates the performance of the proposed method against existing state-of-the-art UCD approaches using the LEVIR-CD dataset. Results indicate that the new model achieves superior performance compared to current methods, while also demonstrating that UCD attains results comparable to supervised change detection (SCD) despite utilizing significantly less data.

Density scaling serves as a robust method for mapping the viscosity of non-associating molecular fluids, yet its application to associating fluids remains debated. This study examines the density scaling of viscosity for the associating fluid 2,2'-methylenebis(4-methyl-6-tert-butylphenol) (BHT) using the SPC/E model, which incorporates explicit hydrogen bonding. Our findings indicate that density scaling is not a reliable approach for BHT. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the density scaling exponent for BHT is highly sensitive to the specific hydrogen bonding model employed.

This study examines a periodic cosmology model featuring a cyclic alternation between $\Lambda$CDM and inflationary phases. We demonstrate that the Universe's behavior in the inflationary epoch is governed by the preceding $\Lambda$CDM era, specifically through the value of the dark energy equation of state. Furthermore, we show that the Universe's expansion rate during the subsequent $\Lambda$CDM phase is determined by the inflationary phase's equation of state.

This paper examines the relationship between counter-factual reasoning and the concept of measurement independence, which is often termed "free will." We demonstrate that counter-factuals and measurement independence are distinct, and we argue that the debate surrounding counter-factuals is largely irrelevant to the core issues of nonlocality and quantum mechanics.

Neural networks have become a standard tool for solving complex problems across diverse domains. However, their substantial memory and computational demands often restrict their deployment on resource-constrained devices like smart speakers and wearables. To address this, we introduce a new approach that leverages the inherent redundancy in neural networks to shrink their size. Our method employs a novel, differentiable pruning technique that removes entire neurons based on their contribution to the loss function. This process is guided by a new metric called the "neuron importance score," which quantifies how much a specific neuron influences the overall loss. We validate our approach on various architectures, including ResNet, VGG, and AlexNet, demonstrating that it effectively reduces model size while maintaining high accuracy.

We establish a cluster expansion for the dimer model on isoradial graphs, which is isomorphic to the cluster expansion of the eight-vertex model on a planar graph. This isomorphism facilitates a direct, term-by-term comparison with the cluster expansion of the planar Ising model, thereby yielding a cluster expansion for the dimer model. This result serves as a crucial step toward proving the existence of a dimer model cluster expansion, ultimately enabling the demonstration of conformal invariance in the dimer model on isoradial graphs.

This study introduces a novel Group Lasso algorithm designed for variable selection in generalized linear models, accommodating both continuous and categorical data. The method employs a penalty function that shrinks coefficients toward zero based on their proximity to a specific target value, which is determined by the data type. For continuous variables, this target is the mean, whereas for categorical variables, it is the mean of the indicator variables. The algorithm utilizes a proximal gradient approach to solve the resulting optimization problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively selects variables and accurately estimates coefficients.

T-Visor is a lightweight, real-time capable hypervisor designed for embedded systems, offering a flexible scheduling framework that accommodates diverse real-time needs. This framework supports both fixed and dynamic priority scheduling, as well as preemptive and non-preemptive execution modes. Additionally, T-Visor provides a robust mechanism for handling virtual timers, which is essential for real-time applications. The hypervisor also features a dedicated interrupt handling system that ensures precise timing and minimal latency.

This paper introduces a new method for stitching panoramic images using an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) to track camera orientation. The approach leverages IMU data to estimate the camera's rotation, which is then used to align images. The method is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in panoramic stitching.

This study examines the stability of chimera states within oscillator networks featuring a single layer of heterogeneity. We demonstrate that enhancing heterogeneity among oscillators can destabilize chimeras, a finding that contradicts the conventional view that heterogeneity is essential for their emergence. Furthermore, we show that the stability of these states is governed by the interplay between the degree of heterogeneity and the network's topology.

This study investigates the robustness of controllers derived from deep reinforcement learning (RL) and dynamics models trained via maximum likelihood. We demonstrate that enforcing a lower bound on likelihood noise within the dynamics model can enhance the robustness of the resulting RL-learned controllers. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach to estimate the uncertainty of the learned dynamics model, which subsequently enables the construction of robust controllers.

This paper introduces a new class of algebras known as "slice algebras," which are constructed by truncating matrix or tensor algebras associated with quivers. We establish a connection between the representation theory of these slice algebras and the representation theory of their corresponding quivers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the representation theory of a specific subclass of slice algebras is equivalent to the representation theory of a specific type of quiver.

We investigate the entanglement spectrum of random tensor networks (RTNs) by examining the spectrum of the transfer matrix. Our findings indicate that the reflected entanglement spectrum of an RTN differs significantly from the standard Rényi spectrum, which is typically governed by the distribution of bond weights. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reflected entanglement spectrum of an RTN can be described as a superposition of the spectra from random unitary quantum circuits.

This study examines the probability of persistence within large collections of dynamical systems, specifically focusing on the impact of system dimensionality and the number of systems involved. We demonstrate that the likelihood of persistence can be significantly enhanced by introducing a specific type of noise. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework for analyzing the persistence probability in systems governed by linear dynamics with random coefficients.

This work examines the parameter space of real quadratic diffeomorphisms, specifically the family $f_c(x) = c + x^2$ where $c > 0$. We demonstrate that this parameter space is organized by a dense network of periodic orbits, which serve as the fundamental building blocks for its intricate geometry.

This study examines the holonomy of a point particle within the framework of the covariant phase space formalism. We demonstrate that the resulting holonomy in gravity differs fundamentally from that in gauge theories, a distinction that arises from the non-integrability of the gravitational symplectic form.

This paper examines the asymptotic behavior of the cumulative distribution functions for the largest eigenvalues of Wishart matrices, specifically $W_n = X_n X_n^T$, where $X_n$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with independent and identically distributed entries having mean zero and unit variance. We establish that these CDFs converge uniformly to a limiting function as $n$ approaches infinity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the rate of this convergence is $O(n^{-1/2})$.

This study introduces a novel formulation for actual tunneling time (ATT) that is directly linked to spin fluctuations within a quantum system. The proposed method is validated by applying it to a one-dimensional tunneling scenario, where the resulting tunneling time aligns with the predictions of the Bohmian approach.

This study examines the decay of $J/\psi$ mesons into two $D$ mesons and a photon, specifically focusing on the contribution of $P$-wave charmonia. We calculate the amplitudes for the $J/\psi \to \eta_c(2S)D\bar{D}^*\gamma$ and $J/\psi \to \chi_{c0,2}D\bar{D}^*\gamma$ processes, incorporating relativistic corrections to the wave functions. Our findings indicate that these corrections significantly affect the amplitudes for $P$-wave charmonia, whereas their impact on the $S$-wave $\eta_c(2S)$ amplitude is negligible.

We introduce a nonlinear Hadamard gate designed for Bose-Einstein condensates, which enables Ramsey interferometry to surpass the standard quantum limit. This approach is realized through a nonlinear Hadamard gate that maps the spinor state of a BEC onto a nonlinear optical state. Subsequent interferometry is performed by measuring the spinor state's population distribution. We demonstrate that this method achieves a phase sensitivity scaling of $1/N^2$, where $N$ represents the number of atoms.

We investigate the asymptotic symmetries of the Einstein-Maxwell theory in four dimensions, specifically within the context of the eBMS algebra. Our analysis reveals that the degeneracies among vacuum states correspond to soft photon modes and a new type of mode analogous to the Schwarzian mode found in gravity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associated eBMS charges are degenerate, with this degeneracy linked to the vacuum's degeneracy. Finally, we establish that the entropy of a black hole can be recovered by counting the states within a specific eBMS orbit.

This study introduces a novel ensemble approach for training neural networks that achieves superior classification accuracy compared to standard techniques. The method operates by training a single neural network on a dataset, then generating a new, augmented version of that dataset by applying random transformations to the original images. This process is repeated multiple times to create several distinct augmented datasets. Subsequently, the network is trained independently on each of these datasets. The final ensemble model is constructed by aggregating the outputs of the individual networks trained on these varied datasets.

Let $F$ be a finite field and $n$ a positive integer. A polynomial function $f: F^n \to F$ is termed a complete mapping if the mapping $x \mapsto f(x) + x$ is a bijection. This study establishes a sufficient condition for a polynomial function to be a complete mapping and provides a complete characterization of complete mappings for functions defined on $F^1$ and $F^2$.

Intestinal parasites are a significant global health concern, yet diagnosing them via human visual inspection of stool samples is prone to high error rates. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to automatically identify and classify these parasites from microscopic images. The proposed method utilizes a multi-task learning approach that simultaneously performs detection and classification. It employs a multi-scale feature fusion strategy to integrate information from various layers of the network, thereby enhancing the model's ability to handle diverse parasite sizes. Furthermore, the system incorporates a novel loss function that addresses class imbalance by assigning higher weights to underrepresented classes. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves a mean average precision (mAP) of 91.2% and an overall classification accuracy of 98.1%.

This study addresses the numerical solution of nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, which arise in the context of zero-sum stochastic differential games. We establish a comparison principle for these equations and demonstrate the existence of viscosity solutions. Furthermore, we introduce a numerical scheme based on the dynamic programming principle to approximate these solutions. The convergence of this scheme is proven, and numerical experiments are provided to validate the findings.

This study introduces a novel control architecture for quadcopters that integrates a Genetic Filter (GF) with a Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR). The Genetic Filter functions as a state estimator, utilizing a genetic algorithm to adaptively tune its parameters in response to disturbances and model uncertainties. Simulation results demonstrate that this combined approach significantly enhances the quadcopter's control performance.

The pion-nucleon sigma term, $\sigma_{\pi N}$, is a critical quantity for nuclear physics research. This study examines the impact of the nucleon's isovector axial charge, $g_A$, on $\sigma_{\pi N}$ by analyzing the nucleon's scalar form factor, $f_S(Q^2)$, within the framework of QCD sum rules. We employ a dispersion relation to express $f_S(Q^2)$ in terms of its spectral function, which is modeled as a sum of nucleon and $\Delta$-resonance poles alongside a continuum. By applying the QCD sum rules method, we determine the scalar form factor at low momentum transfer ($Q^2$) using the nucleon pole contribution. Our findings indicate that the nucleon pole dominates the scalar form factor at low $Q^2$, and the resulting $\sigma_{\pi N}$ value aligns well with recent experimental data.

The CMS experiment at the LHC has undergone significant upgrades to its silicon pixel detector, which were completed in 2016. These enhancements, including the installation of new sensors and a refined readout system, have substantially improved the detector's performance. This text presents an overview of the upgrades and their resulting impact on the CMS detector.

This study presents a deep learning approach for identifying Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) host galaxies using deep imaging data. We trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) on a dataset of 1,000 AGN hosts and 1,000 non-AGN galaxies, achieving a classification precision of 80%. This accuracy remains consistent across redshift intervals of 0.0 < z < 0.5, 0.5 < z < 1.0, and 1.0 < z < 1.5. Furthermore, we applied the trained model to a sample of 1,000 galaxies from the SDSS DR16 catalog, successfully detecting 1,000 AGN hosts and 1,000 non-AGN galaxies.

This study examines the impact of nuclear short-range correlations (SRC) on the neutron skin thickness of asymmetric nuclei, specifically $^{208}\text{Pb}$ and $^{48}\text{Ca}$. We employ the relativistic mean-field framework, incorporating SRC effects through a momentum-dependent in-medium nucleon-nucleon interaction. Our findings indicate that SRC significantly influence neutron skin thickness, with the magnitude of this effect varying across different nuclear models.

This study introduces a novel approach to represent RGB images using complex-valued scaling, which effectively mitigates hue shifts and enhances the correlation between color channels. By employing a complex-valued scaling matrix, the method decomposes an image into two components: a complex-valued scaling matrix and a corresponding complex-valued image matrix. The image matrix is derived by applying the scaling matrix to a reference image. The proposed framework utilizes a complex-valued image matrix constructed from the real and imaginary parts of the image's RGB channels, while the scaling matrix is determined through a specific optimization process. The resulting image matrix is then generated by multiplying the scaling matrix with a reference image. The method's efficacy is validated through experiments on the ImageNet dataset, demonstrating that the reconstructed images exhibit significantly reduced hue shifts and improved inter-channel correlation compared to the original inputs.

The geometrical scaling of the saturation scale, $Q_s^2(x)$, is examined across multiple reactions, including $pp$, $pA$, and $AA$ collisions, as well as $eA$ and $eA$ interactions. This analysis demonstrates that geometrical scaling is a universal feature of gluon distribution saturation, independent of the specific reaction type. Furthermore, the study investigates the geometrical scaling behavior of the saturation scale within the context of the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework.

The initial enrichment of the early galaxy is governed by the mass distribution of core-collapse supernova progenitors, which is stochastic in nature. This distribution is determined by the initial mass function (IMF) of the progenitor stars, which in turn depends on the metallicity of the gas from which they formed. We introduce a novel method to model the progenitor mass distribution that accounts for the IMF's metallicity dependence, utilizing a Bayesian framework to infer the underlying IMF from observed early galaxy abundances. Our results indicate that the progenitor mass distribution is significantly broader than the progenitor IMF, a finding that aligns with the hypothesis that massive stars in the early universe were born in clustered environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the inferred progenitor mass distribution is highly sensitive to the assumed IMF slope, a parameter that is difficult to constrain observationally. Consequently, the progenitor mass distribution serves as a valuable tool for probing the IMF in the early universe.

This study introduces a novel framework for assessing the stability of predictive models, which is defined as the model's performance when augmented with synthetic predictors. We demonstrate that this stability metric is equivalent to the model's out-of-sample prediction error. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical link between stability and the model's generalization error. The proposed methodology is validated through a simulation study and an empirical analysis of a real-world dataset.

Variational quantum models (VQMs) are a prominent class of quantum algorithms that rely on gradient-based optimization to train quantum circuits. A critical unresolved issue is how the choice of output representation influences the scalability of this optimization process. This study investigates the impact of output representation on the scalability of gradient-based optimization within VQMs. We demonstrate that the number of trainable parameters in the gradient vector is a decisive factor for scalability, and we show that this count can be reduced by selecting an appropriate output representation. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for calculating gradients of quantum circuits that is both efficient and scalable.

This study examines the geometry of pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within Sasakian manifolds, specifically analyzing their warping product structures. We establish that such submanifolds, when embedded as warped products, decompose into three orthogonal distributions: one spanned by the Reeb vector field, another by the maximal slant direction, and a third by the maximal anti-slant direction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these pointwise semi-slant submanifolds encompass various known types, including anti-invariant, CR, pointwise invariant, and pointwise anti-invariant submanifolds. Finally, we derive several characterizations for these submanifolds situated in Sasakian space forms.

The Coherent Elastic Neutrino Nucleus Scattering (CEvNS) process, characterized by a low energy threshold, offers a promising avenue for detecting neutrinos from diverse sources. This study introduces a novel, high-efficiency, and low-threshold CEvNS detection method utilizing a liquid scintillator doped with a heavy nucleus. The approach relies on identifying the distinct quenching factor of the heavy nucleus to isolate CEvNS signals from the background of electron scattering. The research details the development of a new liquid scintillator enriched with Xenon and outlines the experimental setup and data analysis techniques employed. Furthermore, the study presents the initial results of a CEvNS search using this new detector, which has been exposed to a neutrino flux from the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

This study examines the dynamics of active dimers, which are composed of two spherical particles linked by a spring and driven by a constant torque. We demonstrate that the motion of these microscopic systems can be effectively modeled as a macroscopic device featuring a steering wheel, where the wheel's rotation angle corresponds to the spring's orientation. This analogy allows us to derive the probability distribution for the dimers' velocity and mean squared displacement. Furthermore, we show that the motion of such dimers can be described by a generalized Langevin equation, with the associated memory kernel derived from the system's microscopic properties.

We investigate the magnetorotronic properties of the $
u=2/7$ fractional quantum Hall state, which is believed to be a chiral bosonic state. Our findings indicate that the magnetorotons in this state exhibit the same chirality as those in the $
u=2/9$ state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnetorotons in the $
u=2/7$ state possess a significantly larger effective mass compared to those in the $
u=2/9$ state.

This study examines the evolution of a stochastic epidemic model on a general contact network, where the state is defined by the infection status of each node. We demonstrate that the concept of equitable partitions, originally developed for deterministic epidemic models, can be extended to the stochastic framework. Specifically, we show that the relaxation of equitable partitions allows for the analysis of the stochastic Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model across arbitrary contact networks. Furthermore, we establish that the relaxation of equitable partitions serves as a sufficient condition for the existence of a stationary distribution within the stochastic SIS model.

This study examines the performance of biased estimators in reconstructing Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) maps, specifically focusing on the impact of strong point sources. We demonstrate that while these estimators yield unbiased results in the absence of point sources, their presence introduces significant bias in the resulting maps. This distortion manifests as a non-uniform error distribution, where errors are amplified near point sources and suppressed in their vicinity. Furthermore, we show that this error distribution is highly sensitive to the specific characteristics of the point sources. Consequently, we argue that the standard practice of masking point sources prior to map reconstruction is unnecessary and may even degrade the quality of the final CMB maps.

This paper introduces a novel framework for task instruction learning that integrates pedagogical and pragmatic principles. The pedagogical component involves a teacher who generates task instructions, while the pragmatic component consists of a learner who executes them. We propose a new method for the teacher to create instructions by leveraging the learner's past performance history. This approach allows the teacher to adapt to the learner's specific capabilities and knowledge gaps, thereby producing more effective guidance. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework through experiments on the instruction following task, where the learner is a large language model.

Shadow tomography is a recent technique designed to efficiently estimate the expectation values of numerous observables for a quantum state, offering a significant advantage over full quantum state tomography by requiring far fewer measurements. This paper introduces a new shadow tomography protocol that leverages the concept of "quantum shadows" to achieve a more efficient estimation of these expectation values. By utilizing a specific set of random unitary operations, the method generates a compact representation of the quantum state, which can then be used to estimate the expectation values of a large number of observables with high accuracy. The proposed protocol is shown to be more efficient than previous shadow tomography methods, as it requires fewer measurements to achieve the same level of accuracy. Furthermore, the method is demonstrated to be robust against noise, making it a promising approach for practical quantum state estimation.
This paper examines the geometric properties of the inradius and circumradius within the context of convex bodies.

This study addresses the challenge of designing trajectories for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) tasked with delivering services to a set of users, where each user is associated with a specific service duration. The objective is to maximize the total number of users served within a fixed time limit. This problem is modeled as a variant of the orienteering problem, which is known to be NP-hard. To tackle this, we introduce a novel algorithm that combines a greedy strategy with a dynamic programming approach. The proposed method is evaluated against existing solutions using both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We investigate the electronic properties of bilayer graphene subjected to a moiré potential, focusing on the interplay between lattice and moiré symmetries. Our analysis reveals that the nematic state, characterized by a reduction in lattice rotational symmetry from $C_4$ to $C_2$, emerges as a stable ground state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system can undergo a transition into a chiral state, which breaks both time-reversal and lattice rotational symmetries.

This study investigates the adsorption of endofullerene molecules onto a graphene substrate using density functional theory (DFT). We demonstrate that the molecule's conformation significantly influences its magnetic and electric characteristics. Furthermore, we show that the graphene substrate can effectively suppress the magnetic moment of the encapsulated molecule.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has heightened concerns regarding data security and privacy. This paper introduces a novel, lightweight, and privacy-preserving framework designed to secure IoT data transmission. The proposed architecture employs a blockchain-based distributed ledger to ensure data integrity and utilizes a secure multi-party computation (SMPC) protocol to safeguard user privacy. Furthermore, the system leverages a distributed consensus mechanism to maintain trust among IoT devices. The study concludes by outlining the framework's key features and presenting a comprehensive evaluation of its performance.

We introduce a Bayesian experiment design framework for optimizing Ramsey measurements in the presence of low-fidelity data. This approach surpasses both adaptive heuristic and random protocols by delivering superior parameter estimation and reduced computational costs. Furthermore, the method is highly versatile, accommodating various noise models and measurement fidelities.

Gromov centrality is a recently introduced metric that quantifies a node's centrality based on its distance from the network's periphery. This study investigates the node classification capabilities of Gromov centrality across diverse network types, including both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our findings indicate that Gromov centrality effectively distinguishes between different node categories in various networks, with performance varying according to the specific network structure.

This study examines the gravitational interaction between the Sun and Earth, incorporating the effects of the Sun's rotation and the Earth's orbital motion. The resulting theory aligns with the observed secular increase in the mean Earth-Sun distance and accounts for the precession of the perihelion. Additionally, the theory predicts a specific secular variation in the Earth's orbital eccentricity.
We demonstrate that bundles of matrix polynomials constitute an open subset within their closure regarding spectral data.

In non-geometric string theory, T-duality is modeled as a Morita equivalence between twisted spectral triples, with the twisted algebra representing the background geometry. This study examines the implications of continuous-trace algebras for the existence of classical T-duals. We demonstrate that when a twisted spectral triple possesses a classical T-dual, the associated twisted algebra must be finite-dimensional. Consequently, this finding indicates that continuous-trace algebras cannot describe classical T-dualizable backgrounds.

We introduce a novel embedding technique that maps graphs with bounded genus into low-dimensional Euclidean spaces while maintaining metric distortion proportional to the square root of the logarithm of the graph's treewidth. This approach yields a significant improvement in the running time for metric Baker's algorithms on minor-free graphs, accelerating them from $O(\log^2 n)$ to $O(\log n)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this embedding facilitates a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the Steiner Tree problem in minor-free graphs, achieving a runtime of $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$.

This study examines the long-term behavior of time-periodic parabolic equations with time-periodic boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the set of initial conditions leading to convergence toward a time-periodic solution is prevalent. Furthermore, we establish that the basin of attraction for this solution is open.

The Qubit Excitation-Based Adaptive Variational Quantum Eigensolver (QEB-ADAPT-VQE) is a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm designed to determine the ground state energy of a system. This protocol integrates the adaptive operator selection mechanism of fermionic-ADAPT-VQE with the excitation-based operator selection of qubit-ADAPT-VQE. By utilizing the excitation-based approach, the method effectively reduces the number of required operators, thereby lowering the circuit depth and the count of variational parameters. Furthermore, the protocol's efficiency is enhanced by a hybrid optimization strategy that combines classical and quantum optimizers. Numerical simulations indicate that QEB-ADAPT-VQE achieves faster convergence and superior performance compared to both fermionic-ADAPT-VQE and qubit-ADAPT-VQE.

The Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) is a generative model capable of learning a latent representation space that maintains a class-separated structure when trained on labeled data. This study investigates the DGD's application to unsupervised learning using unlabeled data. We demonstrate that the DGD can successfully learn a class-separated latent space even without labels, provided the data originates from a mixture of Gaussians. Furthermore, we show that the DGD can be trained on unlabeled data to produce a generative model that accurately captures the underlying data distribution.

We introduce a cosmological model featuring a stiff component that evolves as $w=1$ and a dark energy component with a constant equation of state $w=-1$. This stiff component is proposed as a solution to the Hubble tension, which arises from the discrepancy between early and late universe measurements of the Hubble constant. By analyzing the model's evolution, we find that the stiff component's energy density peaks at a redshift of approximately $z \approx 1000$ and subsequently declines, eventually becoming negligible. Consequently, the model effectively mimics the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework at both high and low redshifts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model can resolve the Hubble tension while remaining consistent with current observational data.

This study presents the first detection of HCN in the coma of comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) using the IRAM 30m telescope, alongside observations of CS, H$_2$CO, HNC, and CH$_3$OH. The derived production rates for these species are compared with data from other comets to evaluate their outgassing behavior. The results indicate that HCN exhibits a distinct outgassing pattern compared to CS, H$_2$CO, HNC, and CH$_3$OH, which are released from deeper within the nucleus. Additionally, the HCN/CH$_3$OH abundance ratio in this comet is significantly lower than that observed in other comets.

This study investigates the potential for unsupervised speech synthesis using a variational autoencoder (VAE) trained on a single speaker's data. The system was evaluated on the TIMIT corpus, with the VAE's latent space conditioned on speaker identity, gender, and phoneme context. Results indicate that the generated speech is both natural and intelligible, though it exhibits a higher degree of variability than that produced by supervised models. Furthermore, the system successfully learns a disentangled representation of the latent space, enabling the generation of diverse utterances for a specific speaker through the manipulation of latent variables.

This study examines the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, which incorporates an interacting coupling parameter. We demonstrate that this coupling parameter is directly linked to the model's constant parameter, a relationship that allows us to derive the equation of state for dark energy. Furthermore, we analyze the model's stability and its behavior within the context of cosmic evolution.

This paper introduces a novel metric called the Investment Ratio (IR) to assess the quality of solutions generated by optimization algorithms. The IR quantifies the computational resources required to achieve a specific solution quality, defined as the ratio of the cost incurred by the algorithm to the cost of the best possible solution. We demonstrate that this metric is applicable to a broad spectrum of optimization challenges, including the Traveling Salesman Problem, the Knapsack Problem, and the Maximum Clique Problem. Furthermore, we present a theoretical framework for IR and establish its relationship with the concept of approximation ratios.

This paper introduces a synthetic differential geometry framework for groupoids, establishing a synthetic analogue of the classical smooth groupoid. We define the source and target maps, along with the source and target path spaces, and demonstrate that the collection of these path spaces forms a simply connected groupoid. Furthermore, we establish a synthetic version of the fundamental theorem of Lie groupoids, which asserts that a smooth groupoid is uniquely determined by its underlying groupoid of paths.

This paper introduces Dynaswap, a secure workflow system designed to facilitate the exchange of data between two parties. The system integrates multiple security protocols, including a blockchain-based timestamping service, a secure multi-party computation protocol, and a blockchain-based smart contract. These components collectively ensure the confidentiality of exchanged data, the integrity of the workflow, and the prevention of double-spending. Furthermore, the Dynaswap project is implemented as a decentralized application (dApp) on the Ethereum blockchain, allowing users to access the system via a web interface.

This study introduces a novel approach to sentiment analysis that leverages Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (SCoP) to enhance the capture of sentiment orientation within product reviews. We demonstrate that SCoP significantly improves the model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative sentiments by learning more discriminative representations. Furthermore, we propose a new metric, the Sentiment Orientation Score (SOS), to evaluate the quality of these representations. Experimental results indicate that integrating SCoP into sentiment analysis models yields substantial performance gains.

The study investigates the impact of gastric acid suppressors on the development of listeriosis, a severe illness caused by *Listeria monocytogenes*. It is established that reduced immunocompetence, often resulting from acid suppression, facilitates the onset of this disease. The research employs a mathematical model to simulate the infection process, incorporating a specific threshold for gastric acidity below which the pathogen can successfully colonize the stomach. The model's parameters were calibrated using data from a clinical trial involving 100 healthy volunteers who consumed a contaminated food product. The findings indicate that the model accurately reflects the observed infection rates, and the results suggest that the elevated incidence of listeriosis among gastric acid suppressor users is primarily driven by the increased likelihood of gastric colonization.

This study investigates the secrecy performance of a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted multiuser communication system, accounting for hardware impairments (HIs) at both the transmitter and receiver. The work begins by deriving the closed-form outage probability for RIS-aided secure links, followed by the development of a low-complexity, efficient RIS configuration algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of outage probability and computational efficiency.

This paper introduces a novel approach to summarization termed "hindsight summarization," which aims to reduce attended prediction error. The method is grounded in the hypothesis that an agent's ability to predict its own future actions is essential for effective learning. We demonstrate that this concept can be applied to create summaries of video sequences. Specifically, we propose a model that learns to generate a summary by predicting the actions required to replay the full original video. We evaluate this model on the MSR-VTT dataset and show that it produces summaries that are both concise and semantically meaningful.

This study examines the energy distributions of energetic particles detected by the STEREO spacecraft, specifically focusing on the relationship between heliocentric distance and the energy required to escape solar gravity. The analysis utilizes data from the STEREO/SECCHI instrument, which recorded particle events during the 2012 July 23 coronal mass ejection (CME) and subsequent solar energetic particle (SEP) event. The findings indicate that the energy distributions for particles at small heliocentric distances are nearly identical to those observed at 1 AU, suggesting that the radial transport of energetic particles is governed by a constant acceleration mechanism.

We establish a connection between the freeness of a locally trivial action of a group $G$ on a C*-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and the freeness of the induced action of $G$ on the associated C*-algebra of equivariant sections. This result serves as a C*-algebraic analogue to the relationship between the freeness of a group action on a topological space and the freeness of the induced action on the algebra of continuous functions.

We demonstrate that the existence of $P$-points is equivalent to the consistency of the inequality $2^{\aleph_0} < 2^{\aleph_1}$. Furthermore, we establish that the consistency of $2^{\aleph_0} < 2^{\aleph_1}$ implies the existence of a model where every real number is a Ramsey real.

This study examines the quantum characteristics of a $q$-deformed optical system featuring a two-level atom interacting with a single-mode cavity field and a mechanical oscillator. The system is driven by a probe field, and the resulting probe transmission spectrum is analyzed. Results indicate that adjusting the tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling significantly influences the probe field. Furthermore, the study explores the generation of nonclassical states within the $q$-deformed cavity mode, demonstrating that the atomic state can be tuned to produce either a $q$-deformed Fock state or a $q$-deformed coherent state.

The study of R-negative states in the $^{136}$Xe nucleus, which are predicted to be the mirror counterparts of R-positive scissors modes, is examined. These R-negative states are expected to exhibit significantly weaker electromagnetic transition strengths compared to their R-positive counterparts. The analysis utilizes the interacting boson-fermion model to calculate the properties of these states, with results compared against experimental data.

This study introduces a neural network-based approach for solving nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws, specifically tailored to capture contact discontinuities and wave phenomena. The method employs a neural network to approximate the solution, with its gradient computed via automatic differentiation. To enforce the conservation law, a penalty term is integrated into the loss function, driving the network to converge toward a valid solution. The approach is validated on the linear advection equation and the Burgers' equation, demonstrating its ability to accurately resolve wave propagation and shock structures.

The LHCb experiment is designed to investigate the small-x gluon distribution within the proton by analyzing forward charm production in proton-proton collisions. This study examines how the proposed LS3 upgrades, which include a new vertex locator and a new RICH detector, enhance the experiment's capabilities. These improvements enable the measurement of the charm cross-section with a precision of 10% and the determination of the charm polarization with a 20% accuracy.

We demonstrate that a time-dependent $\Lambda$-system can detect the timelike Unruh effect. This detection is achieved by measuring the system's time evolution, which reveals the presence of a timelike Rindler vacuum.

Event Extraction (EE) involves identifying and locating event triggers and arguments within a text. While recent advancements have significantly improved performance in English, these methods struggle to generalize to other languages. This limitation stems from the scarcity of annotated data and the lack of suitable pre-trained language models for those languages. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages multilingual pre-trained models to enhance EE performance. Specifically, we propose a new framework that utilizes a multilingual model to generate contextual embeddings for event triggers and arguments, which are then fed into a specialized event extraction model. Our experiments demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art results on the Chinese FinEvent dataset and performs competitively on the German FinEvent dataset.
We establish the positivity of Chern forms as polynomials and utilize this result to address Griffiths' conjecture regarding positive characteristic forms.

We present a multi-wavelength study of the high-mass X-ray binary 4U 1700-37, which is in a low state, utilizing data from the Swift X-ray Telescope, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, and the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. Our analysis reveals that the hard X-ray and soft gamma-ray emission are dominated by a single component, whereas the soft X-ray band arises from a combination of two distinct sources. We observe a significant reduction in coherence between the hard X-ray and gamma-ray light curves, a phenomenon we attribute to the hard X-ray emission being modulated by the binary's orbital period. Furthermore, the hard X-ray and gamma-ray spectra exhibit a power-law distribution with a photon index of approximately 2.0, which remains consistent across the entire energy range.

We investigate the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and the non-abelian Casimir effect within a non-abelian aether framework. The non-abelian aether term, which violates Lorentz invariance, is a non-derivative operator that modifies the non-abelian gauge field's kinetic term. This study demonstrates that the non-abelian aether term alters the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and the non-abelian Casimir effect.

This study examines the syntax-semantics interface through a joint modeling approach, analyzing how linguistic patterns emerge across various languages. We introduce a new framework that integrates a probabilistic context-free grammar with a probabilistic semantic representation, utilizing a shared latent space to connect syntactic and semantic structures. By employing a variational inference method, we can jointly estimate the model's parameters and latent variables. We demonstrate the model's efficacy by applying it to a corpus of 1,000 sentences from English, German, and Dutch. Our findings reveal that the model successfully captures cross-linguistic phenomena, including agreement, word order, and semantic composition. Furthermore, we show that the learned latent space effectively captures semantic relationships, such as synonymy and antonymy, across all three languages.

We introduce a new class of transients powered by radioactivity, resulting from the merger of compact objects. These events are characterized by luminosity peaks ranging from $10^{41}$ to $10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and durations of approximately 100 days. They are expected to occur in the same environments as short gamma-ray bursts, yet they lack a prompt high-energy emission component. We propose that these events are responsible for the majority of the observed population of fast optical transients, which are currently unexplained.

We have conducted a systematic investigation of tidal features in early-type galaxies (ETGs) by analyzing the Hubble Space Telescope's CANDELS survey, which covers 150 square degrees of the sky. Our study identified 1,000 ETGs with stellar masses exceeding $10^{10} M_{\odot}$ and magnitudes fainter than $M_{AB} = -19.5$ within a redshift range of $0.1 < z < 0.5$. We measured the flux fraction of these tidal features and found that they are more prevalent in low-mass ETGs compared to high-mass ones. Additionally, we observed that the flux fraction increases with redshift, a trend that aligns with the known rise in galaxy merger rates. Our findings indicate that approximately 10% of ETGs in the CANDELS field exhibit tidal features, with a flux fraction of roughly 1% for those features.

The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG) is a relativistic framework that models the gravitational field of a rotating, axially symmetric, and stationary mass distribution. This theory is constructed to address the Radiation Problem inherent in General Relativity, which arises from the lack of a consistent mechanism for energy loss in stationary spacetimes. By introducing a novel concept of "gravitational radiation" within a stationary context, ASTG enables the calculation of energy dissipation rates for massive stars during their formation. This capability allows the theory to determine the precise mass of a star at the moment of its birth, thereby resolving the Radiation Problem. Furthermore, ASTG offers a solution to the "Missing Mass Problem" by proposing that the universe contains a significant quantity of dark matter, which is hypothesized to be composed of primordial black holes.

The recent detection of FRB 200428, a repeating fast radio burst, by the CHIME/FRB telescope was accompanied by simultaneous optical observations from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). These optical data, combined with FRB 200428's unique properties, significantly narrow the viable parameter space for emission models. This study examines the implications of these observations for the FRB 200428 source, specifically analyzing the constraints they place on the optical emission mechanisms and the physical characteristics of the source. We explore the feasibility of detecting optical counterparts to FRBs and assess the potential for future FRB 200428 observations to yield further insights into the nature of these events.

Modeling CPA and NLO-based laser systems is a difficult task because it involves numerous parameters and complex physical phenomena. This paper presents a new, simplified model for NLO laser systems that is both easy to use and highly accurate. The model's validity is confirmed by comparing its predictions with experimental data from a Ti:Sapphire laser system.

We introduce MAGIC, a novel framework designed to generate image-conditioned text that maintains both contextual relevance and semantic alignment with the input image. To achieve this, we employ a novel attention mechanism that dynamically balances the influence of the image and the context. Furthermore, we propose a new loss function that explicitly penalizes inconsistencies between the generated output and the provided context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in generating text that is simultaneously coherent with the context and accurately reflective of the image content.

This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a novel privacy-preserving protocol for cryptocurrencies that enhances transaction throughput and scalability. By leveraging a delegation mechanism, the protocol enables the creation of stealth addresses and the generation of valid signatures for these addresses without requiring the original private key. This approach allows for the use of a single private key to generate numerous stealth addresses, thereby reducing the computational overhead associated with verifying signatures. Consequently, the protocol achieves a significant reduction in transaction size and verification time.

The precise measurement of beam-beam closed orbit shifts (BCOS) enables the direct observation of beam-beam effects, including the shift of the resonance driving term and the resonance shift. This study presents the first measurement of the beam-beam resonance shift in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) using BCOS data from the 2018 heavy-ion run. The results align with predictions from the BBCode model, which incorporates the beam-beam resonance shift.

This study introduces a novel approach to address the challenges of history-dependent plasticity in solid mechanics, specifically focusing on the need for continual learning. The method utilizes a neural network to predict the evolution of internal variables, which are subsequently integrated into a finite element framework. A key innovation is the use of a shared neural network architecture across all training tasks, with the network's weights initialized from the final state of the previous task. This strategy enables the model to learn from a continuous sequence of plasticity problems, effectively capturing the material's plastic behavior. The approach is validated through numerical simulations of a uniaxial tension test and a plane strain indentation test.

This study examines the $B\bar{B}^*\pi$ and $B\bar{B}\pi\pi$ invariant mass spectra from the $e^+e^-\to B\bar{B}\pi\pi$ process, utilizing data collected by the BESIII experiment at the $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV energy level. The analysis employs a model-independent approach to extract the $e^+e^-\to B\bar{B}\pi\pi$ cross-section, which is subsequently fitted using a $B\bar{B}\pi\pi$ amplitude model. The resulting fit reveals a clear $\epsilon(10753)$ resonance, which is consistent with a conventional bottomonium state.

Quantized neural networks (QNNs) are a promising avenue for deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices, yet their training remains challenging due to the non-differentiable nature of quantization. While recent approaches like Straight-Through Estimator (STE) have enabled training by approximating quantization as a pass-through operation, they often fail to capture the true distribution of quantized weights, leading to suboptimal performance. This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel stochastic gradient descent variant that corrects the STE's bias by modeling the quantization distribution as asymmetric. By incorporating this asymmetry into the gradient update rule, AskewSGD achieves superior results on QNNs. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that AskewSGD surpasses standard SGD and STE methods, delivering up to a 1.5% accuracy improvement on ImageNet for ResNet-50 and 1.2% for ResNet-101. Furthermore, it outperforms existing baselines by 1.5% to 2.5% across various architectures and datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet.

Continuum soft robots are increasingly utilized in applications requiring complex, adaptable movements. Unlike the segmented limbs found in vertebrates and invertebrates, these robots feature continuous, flexible structures that can be engineered to mimic the kinematics of biological systems. This study introduces a novel design methodology for soft robots that replicates the kinematic behavior of a specific animal's limb. The approach involves creating a continuum robot with a variable cross-section, where the relationship between the section's geometry and the resulting curvature is defined by a polynomial function. By employing a finite element model, the research derives the polynomial coefficients necessary to match the target kinematic profile. The methodology is validated through the design of a soft robot that emulates the kinematics of a lobster claw, with results confirming that the proposed design achieves the desired kinematic performance.

We establish a correspondence between left-invariant metrics on the Jacobi group that are Einstein with respect to the Jacobi-Lie bracket and Kähler balanced metrics on the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane.

This study introduces a novel approach to fact verification that involves breaking down complex assertions into simpler, verifiable sub-statements. By utilizing a graph-based decomposition model, we convert the original task into a multi-step process where each sub-statement is verified individually. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy significantly boosts performance on both the FEVER and FEVEROUS datasets. Furthermore, our method offers a more interpretable verification process, as it explicitly identifies the specific sub-statements that support or refute the original claim.

Generative models are increasingly vital for creating synthetic data, yet they typically depend on large volumes of annotated information. This study introduces a new framework that enables the generation of data from unstructured sources without requiring any annotations. By employing a two-stage approach, the method first learns a latent representation of the data distribution and subsequently utilizes this representation to synthesize new samples. The approach is validated across three distinct domains: images, text, and graphs.

This paper introduces a novel approach to slice sampling that combines the advantages of hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling. The proposed method is more efficient than standard slice sampling, whitened slice sampling, and hit-and-run algorithms. Additionally, it is straightforward to implement and can be applied to a broad range of problems.

We introduce a novel approach to the fault-tolerant all-pairs shortest path problem, which involves precomputing fault-tolerant distance labels for every vertex in a graph. These labels enable the calculation of the shortest path distance between any two vertices even if a single vertex fails. Our method achieves a preprocessing time of $O(mn)$ and a query time of $O(n)$, where $m$ and $n$ represent the number of edges and vertices, respectively. This performance is optimal regarding query time and nearly matches the best-known preprocessing time for the standard all-pairs shortest path problem.

We investigate the two-particle correlation functions of a driven Bose-Hubbard model, which exhibits a dissipative phase transition (DPT) between a superfluid and a Mott insulator. By analyzing the HBT correlation functions, we demonstrate that their Fourier transforms reveal the DPT's critical characteristics. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the HBT correlation length and the system's correlation length.

This paper establishes solvability for the Dirichlet problem concerning linear elliptic equations within a bounded domain characterized by a small Lipschitz constant. The solution's regularity is quantified by a weighted norm, where the weight is a power of the distance to the boundary. The exponent of this weight is determined by the equation's coefficients and the boundary's geometry.

This study introduces a novel, fully automatic method for segmenting brain tissues in MRI scans, grounded in a Gaussian Process framework that models the smoothness of tissue boundaries. By leveraging the inherent smoothness of these contours, the approach effectively mitigates the impact of noise and artifacts. Furthermore, the method incorporates a prior distribution of tissue boundaries derived from a training set of manually segmented images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in cases involving noisy or artifact-laden data.

We investigate the emergence of Bose condensation in a one-dimensional Bose gas subjected to periodic driving and coupled to a thermal bath. Our analysis reveals that the interaction between dissipation and Floquet heating can generate a non-equilibrium steady state (NESS) featuring a condensate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the condensate's stability is contingent upon the interplay between the driving frequency and the bath temperature.

This paper examines the regularity of convex functions within the framework of the space of functions of bounded variation ($BV$). We establish that a convex function $f$ belongs to the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}$ if and only if the exponent $p$ is less than or equal to $\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the infimum of the exponents $p$ for which the $L^p$ norm of the Hessian of $f$ remains finite. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the regularity of such functions is governed by the regularity of their Hessian.

This study examines the impact of photodetection on the performance of clocks utilizing two-level quantum systems. We demonstrate that photodetection can enhance clock performance by reducing the quantum backaction noise affecting the system's phase. Furthermore, we show that the optimal detection efficiency for maximizing performance is not necessarily unity.

This study introduces a novel Heuristic OFES (HFES) algorithm designed to optimize energy consumption and reliability within Optical Burst Switching (OBS) networks. The proposed method leverages the concept of an Energy Reliability Path (ERP) to identify the most energy-efficient and reliable routes for burst transmission. By integrating a heuristic approach, the algorithm effectively balances energy usage and reliability, ensuring that the resulting paths are both efficient and dependable. Simulation results indicate that the HFES algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of energy efficiency and reliability, making it a promising solution for future OBS networks.

This study introduces a novel gradient-based approach for image retrieval that leverages the decomposition of the pair-wise loss function. By separating the gradient into two distinct components, the method isolates the influence of anchor and positive samples from that of the anchor and negative samples. This separation enables the independent optimization of each component, thereby enhancing the model's discriminative capability. Furthermore, the approach facilitates the integration of various loss functions, such as the triplet loss, into the framework. Empirical evaluations on the CUB-200-2011 and Flickr30k datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

We investigate the properties of tensor networks that function as erasure correction codes. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a network comprises only one type of tensor, it must be a stabilizer code. Furthermore, we establish that any such network with a single tensor type and a non-degenerate code distance is necessarily a graph state.

Magnetized radio filaments are a common feature in the radio halos and relics of galaxy clusters. While their origins remain debated, two primary mechanisms are suggested: either they form from the magnetic field lines of the halo itself or they arise from the magnetic field lines of the relic. This study investigates the magnetic field line structure of the radio halo in the Perseus cluster using the MHD code RAMSES. We find that the filamentation observed in the halo is not caused by the magnetic field lines of the halo, but rather by the magnetic field lines of the relic. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the filamentation in the halo aligns with the magnetic field lines of the relic, which are in turn parallel to the relic's morphology. This paper introduces a distributed control framework designed to manage distributed energy resources (DERs) within a microgrid. The proposed method utilizes a leader-follower control strategy, where designated leaders are responsible for regulating DERs, while followers handle the control of loads. The system's primary objective is to ensure that the aggregate power output from DERs matches the total power consumption of the loads. The control architecture relies on local measurements and communication with neighboring agents, eliminating the need for a central controller. Furthermore, the system is engineered to remain resilient against communication failures and the loss of leader agents.

This study investigates the multi-armed bandit problem under the assumption that arm pulls may result in either loss or delay. We introduce a novel framework termed the "lossy and delayed bandit problem," which encompasses various existing models as special cases. Our primary contribution is a regret bound that explicitly accounts for the frequency of losses and delays associated with the optimal arm. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm, LossyDelayedUCB, which achieves this regret bound.

This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for dialogue text generation, which is grounded in the concept of a dialogue state. We demonstrate that this approach offers a unified and concise representation of various existing models, including those based on reinforcement learning, maximum likelihood estimation, and imitation learning. Furthermore, we establish a formal proof of the optimality of the dialogue state for text generation.

The study of strong-interaction matter has been a central focus in quantum chromodynamics (QCD) for over half a century, with particular attention given to the phase diagram of nuclear matter. This review examines recent experimental and theoretical advancements concerning the QCD phase diagram, specifically highlighting the discovery of a critical point and the existence of a first-order phase transition.

This study examines the stochastic characteristics of loads acting on offshore wind turbines, with a specific focus on the influence of inflow turbulence and irregular waves. The analysis utilizes a 5 MW turbine model situated in 20 m deep water, employing a coupled aero-hydro-servo-elastic simulation framework. The findings indicate that the stochastic behavior of turbine loads is significantly shaped by the stochastic properties of inflow turbulence and irregular waves. Furthermore, the research evaluates the impact of stochastic loads on the fatigue performance of the turbine, revealing that the fatigue damage caused by irregular waves is notably lower than that resulting from inflow turbulence.

This study examines the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) to analyze public sentiment regarding the 2018 Sulawesi earthquake and tsunami in Indonesia. By leveraging Twitter data, the research aims to assess the efficacy of NLP in monitoring public sentiment during disasters. The methodology involves collecting tweets via the Twitter API, filtering for relevant content using keyword searches, and classifying sentiment through a combination of NLP techniques and machine learning. The findings indicate that NLP can effectively gauge public sentiment in disaster contexts, offering valuable insights for emergency response and resource allocation.

The $R$-nilpotency degree of a group $G$ is defined as the smallest integer $n$ such that the $n$-th term of the lower central series of $G$ is contained in $R$. This study investigates the $R$-nilpotency degree of a group $G$ when $R$ is a subgroup of $G$ that is both normal and nilpotent. We establish that if $G$ is a finite group with a nilpotent subgroup $R$ of order $n$, then the $R$-nilpotency degree of $G$ is at most $n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if $G$ is a finite group with a normal subgroup $R$ of order $n$, then the $R$-nilpotency degree of $G$ is at most $n$. Finally, we show that if $G$ is a finite group with a normal subgroup $R$ of order $n$, then the $R$-nilpotency degree of $G$ is at most $n$.

This study introduces a novel inversion technique for the time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-ARPES) method, which is designed to overcome the challenges of retrieving complex-valued electron dynamics from noisy experimental data. The approach utilizes a regularized least-squares framework to solve the inverse problem, incorporating a Tikhonov regularization term to ensure a stable solution. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through numerical simulations and by analyzing actual TR-ARPES data from a cuprate superconductor.

This study introduces a novel approach to analyzing driving scenarios by integrating a Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA) tracker with a Bayesian network. The JPDA tracker is employed to identify and track vehicles, while the Bayesian network models the driving scenario itself. The paper details the methodology for constructing this Bayesian network and outlines the specific parameters used to represent the scenario. Furthermore, the authors present a new metric for quantifying the similarity between two driving scenarios. The proposed method is validated through a case study involving two distinct driving scenarios.

This study examines the reflected entropy within an interface conformal field theory (iCFT) defined on a two-dimensional Euclidean space. We demonstrate that the reflected entropy exhibits universal behavior analogous to the Markov gap in the limit of large subsystems, a phenomenon that persists even when the subsystems are separated by a finite distance. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the reflected entropy and the mutual information in iCFT, revealing that the mutual information displays a universal logarithmic divergence as the subsystems approach one another.

This study introduces a novel channel estimation technique for orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems that leverages the enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM). The proposed method is designed to function effectively under conditions of a cyclic prefix shorter than the channel impulse response and imperfect hardware, such as phase noise and carrier frequency offset. By utilizing the ELM's capability to map input data to output with high accuracy, the approach achieves precise channel estimation. Simulation results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing channel estimation techniques in terms of bit error rate (BER) performance.

Although non-projective measurements are theoretically valid in quantum mechanics, they are often difficult to realize experimentally. This study demonstrates that non-projective measurements can be simulated using projective measurements, provided the outcomes are processed through a specific post-processing method. This approach is particularly advantageous for simulating measurements that are otherwise hard to implement, such as those involving continuous variables.

This paper investigates the rigidity of G2-instantons on R^7 that exhibit abelian behavior at infinity. We demonstrate that such instantons are rigid, meaning they possess no non-trivial infinitesimal deformations.

The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted the rapid deployment of contact tracing technologies, which, while intended to curb viral spread, have also raised significant privacy concerns. This paper examines the privacy risks inherent in these systems, specifically focusing on the potential for mass surveillance by governments and private entities. We argue that the widespread adoption of such technologies could establish a precedent for future mass surveillance, thereby eroding the privacy norms that currently safeguard citizens.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-mode Bose-Hubbard system coupled to a thermal reservoir, with a focus on the interplay between decoherence and entanglement. We demonstrate that, contrary to the standard view, decoherence can facilitate the generation of entanglement between subsystems. Furthermore, we show that the system's ability to reach a steady state is contingent upon the specific values of the coupling constants.

We introduce a language translation framework that converts high-level constructs into a target language, enabling the verification of correctness properties through the target's existing tools. This approach is demonstrated by translating a functional language into a concurrent one, thereby allowing the use of established concurrent verification methods to verify functional programs.

The Iochroma family, a minor asteroid group, was initially identified in 2014. This study presents the results of a search for additional members conducted using the Catalina Real-time Transient Survey (CRTS) data from 2014 to 2018. The analysis identified 10 new candidates, with one confirmed member, 2018 QG10, discovered. Furthermore, the study reports the detection of a new candidate, 2018 QG10, which was confirmed as a member of the Iochroma family. We establish a $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory for the stack of elliptic curves, where $T$ represents the multiplicative group. This theory is constructed by extending the existing $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology defined on the stack of elliptic curves with level structures.

This paper introduces a novel unsupervised learning framework designed to identify and analyze the geometrical structures within data. The approach begins by employing a variational autoencoder to generate a latent representation of the input, which is then utilized to construct a graph where nodes represent data points and edges signify their proximity. Subsequently, a graph convolutional network is applied to this structure to extract features, which are then fed into a clustering algorithm. The efficacy of this method is validated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study examines the $\psi(2S)$ production mechanism in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, focusing on the $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) final states. The analysis utilizes data from the LHCb experiment, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 1 fb$^{-1}$ collected at the LHC. The $\psi(2S)$ is reconstructed via its decay into $J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$. The study reports the first measurements of the $\theta$-parameter for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ production, alongside the first determination of the $\theta$-parameter for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ production. The observed $\theta$-parameter value for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ is found to be approximately 1.5 times larger than that for $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ productions. Additionally, the study presents the first measurement of the $\theta$-parameter for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ production.
